key_terms.meaning: Three-terminal resistor with a sliding wiper; for wiper at distance x on a track of length L, output V₀ = (x/L)·V<sub>s</sub> where V<sub>s</sub> is the supply voltage.
Output volts per unit displacement, S = V<sub>s</sub>/L (V/m) for a linear track, or V<sub>s</sub>/θ<sub>max</sub> for a rotary one.
Fall in output voltage when the measuring circuit draws current; it is nearly zero if the load resistance is far larger than the potentiometer resistance.
Smallest displacement the wiper can distinguish; a wire-wound track with N turns gives resolution ≈ L/N.
A thin metal foil or wire grid bonded to a surface; when the surface stretches or compresses, the grid resistance changes.
GF = (ΔR/R)/(ΔL/L) = (ΔR/R)/ε; about 2 for metal foil gauges, 50 to 200 for semiconductor gauges.
Strain at right angles to the gauge axis also changes resistance; the folded grid shape of a foil gauge cancels most of this error.
Doped silicon bar whose resistance changes strongly with strain through the piezoresistive effect; high GF but strong temperature dependence.
Four-resistor bridge that converts ΔR/R into a voltage; a single active arm gives V₀ ≈ (V<sub>s</sub>/4)·(ΔR/R) at small strain.
A machined elastic element (column, beam or ring) carrying four bonded gauges in a full bridge; a column gives V<sub>s</sub>·GF·ε(1 + ν)/2, a bending beam V<sub>s</sub>·GF·ε.
Gauges fixed at ±45° to the shaft axis measure shear strain; shear stress τ = T·r/J, so torque T follows from the bridge output.
Resistance temperature detector: a pure platinum or nickel winding whose resistance rises almost linearly with temperature.
R<sub>T</sub> = R₀[1 + AT + BT² + C(T − 100)T³], with A = 3.9083 × 10⁻³ /°C and B = −5.775 × 10⁻⁷ /°C² for platinum; C = 0 above 0 °C.
Sintered metal-oxide ceramic with a large negative temperature coefficient; R = R₀·exp[β(1/T − 1/T₀)], with β in kelvin.
A fine heated wire in a flow; King’s law h = a + b√u links its cooling to speed u, and the bridge output follows E² = A + B√u.
A moisture-absorbing film whose resistance falls as water vapour is adsorbed; it is calibrated directly in relative humidity (%RH).
Cadmium sulphide or similar semiconductor whose resistance drops as illuminance E rises, roughly R = A·E<sup>−γ</sup>.
A material such as indium antimonide, or a thin magnetic multilayer, whose resistance rises in a magnetic field; used for contactless position and speed sensing.
Two dissimilar metals joined at two points produce an emf E = S(T<sub>h</sub> − T<sub>c</sub>), where S is the Seebeck coefficient in µV/°C.
Circuit or software that measures the reference junction temperature and adds it back, so the displayed value is the hot-junction temperature.

takeaways: A potentiometer is the simplest displacement sensor: displacement sets the wiper position, the divider sets the voltage, and the only serious error is loading by the measuring circuit.
A strain gauge turns mechanical strain into a fractional resistance change, and the gauge factor is the single constant that links the two.
Metal foil gauges are linear and stable; semiconductor gauges are far more sensitive but need temperature compensation.
The Wheatstone bridge is the standard signal-conditioning circuit for every resistive sensor in this unit, because it reads small ΔR/R without being swamped by the large standing resistance.
Shape the elastic element properly and a strain gauge measures force, weight or torque with a calibration that is fixed by geometry, not by the electronics.
RTDs are accurate and near-linear but slow; thermistors are very sensitive but nonlinear and limited in range; choosing between them is a trade of linearity against sensitivity.
The same resistance–temperature relation that makes a hot wire cool also makes it a flow sensor, which is why hot-wire anemometry is a temperature measurement in disguise.
Photon and magnetic-field sensors are passive resistors with no moving parts, which makes them cheap, rugged and easy to interface to a bridge.
A thermocouple needs no excitation and works to very high temperatures, but its accuracy depends entirely on knowing or compensating the cold junction.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a labelled construction sketch, the governing formula with each symbol defined, a worked numerical example and the practical errors with their remedies; most syllabi also ask for the biomedical uses of strain gauges, thermistors and RTDs.

bank.q: Define gauge factor. Derive its expression for a single metal wire strain gauge using the resistance formula R = ρL/A, and explain why the value for a metal gauge is close to 2.
outline: R = ρL/A written with each symbol defined
Logarithmic differentiation giving ΔR/R = Δρ/ρ + ΔL/L − ΔA/A
Area change from Poisson's ratio: ΔA/A = −2ν·ε
Result GF = 1 + 2ν + (Δρ/ρ)/ε
For metals the resistivity term is small and ν ≈ 0.3, so GF ≈ 2
Comment: semiconductor gauges get their large GF from the resistivity term
answer: Definition. The gauge factor is the fractional change of resistance per unit strain: GF = (ΔR/R)/ε, where R is the unstrained resistance (Ω), ΔR its change (Ω) and ε = ΔL/L the axial strain (dimensionless, often written in µε). A gauge with GF = 2 changes resistance by 2 parts per million for every microstrain.

Starting point. A wire of length L (m), cross-section A (m²) and resistivity ρ (Ω·m) has R = ρL/A. Stretching it changes all three: L grows, A shrinks by the Poisson effect, and ρ itself changes with the stress in the crystal lattice (the piezoresistive effect).

answer.text: Logarithmic differentiation. Take logarithms and differentiate:
answer.pre:
ln R = ln ρ + ln L − ln A
dR/R = dρ/ρ + dL/L − dA/A

answer: The area term. For a round wire of diameter D, A = πD²/4, so dA/A = 2·dD/D. Poisson’s ratio ν links lateral and axial strain: dD/D = −ν·dL/L = −ν·ε. Hence dA/A = −2ν·ε: the area falls as the wire is stretched. The same result holds for a rectangular foil strip, since both width and thickness shrink by ν·ε.

answer.text: Substitute and divide by ε.

answer: Reading the result. The term 1 is the length change, 2ν is the area change, and together 1 + 2ν is the geometric part. The last term (dρ/ρ)/ε is the piezoresistive part, a property of the material.

Why a metal gauge has GF close to 2. For metals ν ≈ 0.3, so the geometric part is 1 + 2 × 0.3 = 1.6. In constantan (the usual foil alloy) the resistivity term adds about 0.4, giving GF ≈ 2.0 to 2.1. Even with no resistivity change at all, a material that kept its volume (ν = 0.5) would give exactly 1 + 1 = 2, so GF near 2 is what geometry alone predicts.

answer.text: Numerical check. A 120 Ω constantan gauge with GF = 2.0 at ε = 1000 µε:

answer: Semiconductor gauges. In p-type silicon the resistivity term dominates: GF is 100 to 150 while the geometric part is still only about 1.6. That makes them fifty times more sensitive than foil, which is why silicon diaphragms carry diffused piezoresistors in disposable blood-pressure transducers, but the same term makes them non-linear and strongly temperature dependent.

Check. With GF = 2.0 a strain of 1000 µε gives ΔR/R = 0.002, so R moves from 120.000 Ω to 120.240 Ω; the change is tiny, which is why gauges are always read in a Wheatstone bridge rather than with an ohmmeter.

bank.q: Describe the construction of a wire-wound and a conductive-film potentiometer used as a displacement sensor. Explain, with a circuit diagram, how the output voltage becomes proportional to displacement and what limits its accuracy.
outline: Former, mandrel, resistance wire or film, wiper, end connections
Circuit as a voltage divider: V₀ = (x/L)·V<sub>s</sub>
Sensitivity S = V<sub>s</sub>/L in V/m
Resolution set by number of turns, L/N
Loading error when the meter resistance is not much larger than the track resistance
Friction, wear, backlash and nonlinearity of the winding
answer: Wire-wound construction. An insulating former (ceramic, glass-filled plastic or an enamelled metal mandrel) carries a single layer of fine resistance wire, usually nickel-chromium or a precious-metal alloy, wound with constant pitch. One edge of the winding is bared and a wiper of phosphor bronze or precious metal presses on it. The two ends of the winding and the wiper are the three terminals. A linear pot has a straight former of stroke L; a rotary pot wraps it into a circle; a multi-turn (helical) pot winds it as a helix for ten turns of the shaft.

Conductive-film construction. A film of carbon-loaded plastic or cermet (ceramic-metal) is printed or moulded on a substrate, with metal end terminations; the wiper is a multi-finger brush. The track is continuous, so there are no turn-to-turn steps, contact noise is lower and life runs to millions of cycles; the price is a larger temperature coefficient of resistance.

answer.text: Circuit diagram. The track of resistance R is fed from Vs; the wiper at distance x from the zero end taps a voltage V0 that a voltmeter of resistance Rm reads.

svg.aria: Potentiometer displacement sensor circuit: a 5 kilohm track of 100 millimetres fed from a 10 volt supply, a wiper at distance x from the zero end, and a 1 megohm voltmeter reading V zero between wiper and zero end.

answer: Why the output is proportional to displacement. For a uniform track the resistance from the zero end to the wiper is R·x/L. With no current drawn by the meter the track is a voltage divider: V0 = Vs·(R·x/L)/R = Vs·x/L = Vs·α, with α = x/L. The sensitivity is S = Vs/L.
Numbers. L = 100 mm, Vs = 10 V: S = 10/100 = 0.1 V/mm. At x = 35 mm, V0 = 0.1 × 35 = 3.5 V. With 500 turns, the resolution is L/N = 100/500 = 0.2 mm and each step is Vs/N = 20 mV.
Limit 1: resolution. A wire-wound track moves in steps of L/N; finer wire raises N but lowers the current rating. A film track is continuous, limited by the wiper size and noise.

Limit 2: loading. A meter of finite Rm draws current from the wiper. With r = R/Rm, V0 = Vs·α/[1 + α(1 − α)·r]. For R = 5 kΩ and Rm = 1 MΩ, r = 0.005 and the error at mid-stroke is 6.2 mV (0.125 % of reading); with a 50 kΩ meter (r = 0.1) it would reach 1.45 % of full scale near two-thirds of the stroke.
Limit 3: linearity of the track. Uneven wire diameter or winding pitch, or uneven film thickness, makes R·x/L only approximately true; good pots are specified to ±0.1 % to ±1 % of full scale.

Limit 4: mechanical effects. Wiper friction loads a light mechanism; backlash in the shaft and wiper gives a dead band on reversal; wear and dirt raise contact resistance and produce noise; vibration makes the wiper bounce. Power rating sets the largest Vs (P = Vs²/R = 100/5000 = 20 mW here).
Check. At x = L the output is Vs and at x = 0 it is 0 V whatever the load; the 20 mV turn step is bigger than the 6.2 mV loading error, so with a 1 MΩ meter resolution, not loading, limits this pot.

bank.q: State and explain the three laws of thermoelectric circuits. Show how the law of intermediate metals allows copper leads to be used in a thermocouple circuit.
outline: Law of homogeneous material: a temperature gradient along one wire alone produces no emf
Law of intermediate metals: an inserted third metal at the same temperature changes nothing
Law of intermediate temperatures: E(T₁,T₃) = E(T₁,T₂) + E(T₂,T₃)
Application of the second law to copper connecting leads and terminal blocks
Practical consequence: only the two junction temperatures matter
answer: Set-up. A thermocouple is two dissimilar metals A and B joined at a hot (measuring) junction at Th and a cold (reference) junction at Tc. The net emf E depends on the two junction temperatures through the Seebeck coefficient S of the pair, E ≈ S(Th − Tc) over a small span. Three empirical laws let us use it in real circuits.

Law 1: homogeneous circuit. A current cannot be sustained in a circuit of a single homogeneous metal by heat alone, however the temperature varies along it. Consequence: the emf of a thermocouple depends only on the junction temperatures, not on the temperature profile along the wires. A type K wire can pass through a 600 °C furnace wall without error, provided the wire is homogeneous; cold work, contamination or oxidation make it inhomogeneous and create spurious emfs.

Law 2: intermediate metals. A third metal C inserted anywhere in the circuit adds no net emf if both of its junctions are at the same temperature. Consequence: a voltmeter, solder, copper terminals and copper leads can be put in the loop.

Law 3: intermediate temperatures. If a pair gives E(T1, T2) between T1 and T2, and E(T2, T3) between T2 and T3, then E(T1, T3) = E(T1, T2) + E(T2, T3). Consequence: tables referred to 0 °C can be used with a cold junction at room temperature.

answer.text: Worked use of law 3 (type K). Table values: E(300 °C, 0) = 12.209 mV, E(30 °C, 0) = 1.203 mV. The meter reads with the cold junction at 30 °C:

answer: Copper leads by law 2. In a real instrument the chromel and alumel wires end on two copper terminals of an input block. This creates two new junctions, chromel–copper and alumel–copper. If both terminals sit at the same temperature Tc, the copper acts as an intermediate metal between them: the loop chromel → copper → alumel behaves exactly as a direct chromel–alumel junction at Tc. The terminal block is therefore the cold junction, and the copper leads, the switch contacts and the meter itself add nothing.

The condition that matters. The two terminals must be at the same temperature. That is why instruments mount them on an isothermal block of copper or aluminium and measure the block’s temperature for compensation. If one terminal is warmed, say by a nearby power resistor, the two copper junctions no longer cancel and the error is a few degrees.

Practical consequence. Together the laws say: only the two junction temperatures matter. Keep the wires homogeneous (law 1), keep every added junction pair isothermal (law 2), and correct for the cold junction with a table value (law 3).
Check. If Tc were ignored, 11.006 mV would read about 270 °C instead of 300 °C, an error close to the 30 °C cold-junction temperature.

bank.q: Compare a platinum RTD, a thermistor and a thermocouple for temperature measurement in the range 0–400 °C under the headings: sensing principle, sensitivity, linearity, range, excitation, speed of response and cost.
outline: RTD: metal resistance rise, near linear, needs excitation current, wide range, moderate cost
Thermistor: ceramic, large negative coefficient, nonlinear, narrow range, needs excitation, fast, cheap
Thermocouple: Seebeck emf, no excitation, very wide range, needs cold-junction compensation
Sensitivity figures: about 0.385 Ω/Ω per °C for Pt, several percent per °C for a thermistor, about 40 µV/°C for a type-K pair
Self-heating in RTD and thermistor but not in thermocouple
Conclusion: match the sensor to range, accuracy and speed needs
answer: Approach. Compare a Pt100 RTD (R0 = 100 Ω), an NTC thermistor (10 kΩ at 25 °C, β = 3500 K) and a type K thermocouple over 0–400 °C under each heading, with numbers.

Sensing principle. RTD: the resistance of pure platinum rises with temperature, RT = R0[1 + AT + BT²]. Thermistor: a sintered metal-oxide ceramic whose resistance falls exponentially, RT = R0·exp[β(1/T − 1/T0)]. Thermocouple: a Seebeck emf from two dissimilar metals, E ≈ S(Th − Tc).

Sensitivity. Pt100: 0.385 Ω/°C on average (0.385 %/°C at 0 °C), falling to 0.345 Ω/°C at 400 °C. Thermistor: (1/R)(dR/dT) = −β/T² = −3500/298.15² = −3.9 %/°C at 25 °C, ten times the RTD. Type K: about 41 µV/°C; 400 °C gives only 16.40 mV.

Linearity. Pt100: R(0) = 100.00 Ω, R(200) = 175.86 Ω, R(400) = 247.09 Ω. The straight line between the ends gives 173.55 Ω at 200 °C, a deviation of 2.31 Ω, about 6 °C or 1.6 % of span, removed by the Callendar–Van Dusen equation. Thermistor: strongly non-linear; from 29.3 kΩ at 0 °C to 945 Ω at 100 °C and 312 Ω at 150 °C. Type K: close to linear, within about 1 % of span here.

Range. Pt100: −200 to 850 °C, so 0–400 °C is easy. Common epoxy or glass-bead NTCs: roughly −50 to 150 °C, special glass types to about 300 °C; at 400 °C the 10 kΩ part would be about 14 Ω, useless. Type K: −200 to about 1250 °C.

Excitation. RTD: a current of about 1 mA, giving 0.1 mW of self-heating at 0 °C. Thermistor: 10–100 µA, kept low because its high sensitivity makes self-heating errors large. Thermocouple: none; it generates its own emf but needs cold-junction compensation.

Speed of response. Bead thermistors and exposed-junction thermocouples have time constants of a fraction of a second; a sheathed RTD probe takes several seconds because the element is larger and packed in powder.
Cost. Thermistor cheapest; thermocouple wire cheap, but the CJC electronics add cost; a class A platinum RTD is moderate to high.

answer.text: Summary.

answer: Conclusion. For 0–400 °C the thermistor is out on range. Choose the Pt100 for accuracy and stability (a process line, a sterilising autoclave at 121–134 °C), and the thermocouple for speed, small size or the upper end of the range at low cost.
Check. 16.40 mV over 400 °C is 41 µV/°C, while the Pt100 changes by 147 Ω over the same span; a 1 mA current turns that into 147 mV, nine times the thermocouple signal.

bank.q: A linear potentiometer has a 100 mm track, a supply of 10 V and a wire winding of 500 turns. Find the sensitivity in V/mm, the output for a wiper at 35 mm, and the resolution in millimetres. The wiper feeds a voltmeter of 1 MΩ and the track resistance is 5 kΩ. Estimate the loading error at mid-travel.
outline: S = V<sub>s</sub>/L = 10/100 = 0.1 V/mm
Resolution = L/N = 100/500 = 0.2 mm
Divider output at mid-travel is 5 V, Thevenin resistance about 1.25 kΩ
Error fraction ≈ R<sub>th</sub>/R<sub>meter</sub> ≈ 0.125 %, about 6 mV
Conclusion: loading error is negligible with a high-impedance meter
answer: Given. L = 100 mm, Vs = 10 V, N = 500 turns, track R = 5 kΩ, meter Rm = 1 MΩ.
Sensitivity. S = Vs/L = 10 V/100 mm = 0.1 V/mm.
Output at 35 mm (ideal). V0 = S·x = 0.1 × 35 = 3.5 V.
Resolution. Δx = L/N = 100/500 = 0.2 mm; the voltage step is Vs/N = 10/500 = 20 mV.

Loading at mid-travel, Thevenin method. At α = 0.5 the open-circuit output is 5 V. Looking back into the wiper, the two halves of the track (2.5 kΩ each) are in parallel: Rth = α(1 − α)R = 0.25 × 5000 = 1250 Ω.

answer.text: Loaded output. The meter forms a divider with Rth:

answer: Same result from the book’s formula. r = R/Rm = 5000/10⁶ = 0.005; k = α(1 − α)r = 0.25 × 0.005 = 0.00125; V0 = 5/(1.00125) = 4.99376 V. The error fraction k/(1 + k) ≈ k = 0.125 %, matching Rth/Rm.

answer.text: Error along the stroke.

answer: Track power. I = Vs/R = 10/5000 = 2 mA; P = 10 × 0.002 = 20 mW, well within a typical rating.
If the meter were poorer. A 50 kΩ meter (r = 0.1) would give k = 0.025 at mid-travel and an output of 5/1.025 = 4.878 V, an error of 122 mV, six turn steps; then a buffer amplifier would be needed.

Conclusion. The loading error (at most about 7 mV, near two-thirds of the stroke) is smaller than one 20 mV turn step, so with a 1 MΩ meter the loading error is negligible and the resolution of 0.2 mm is the real limit.
Check. Both ends are exact (0 V and 10 V), and the 1 MΩ meter is 200 times the track resistance, comfortably above the ten-times rule.

bank.q: A 120 Ω foil strain gauge with gauge factor 2.1 forms one arm of a Wheatstone bridge excited at 4 V. The surface strain is 600 microstrain. Find the resistance change, the open-circuit bridge output, and the output if all four arms are active with two in tension and two in compression.
outline: Quarter-bridge output V₀ = (V<sub>s</sub>/4)·GF·ε = 1.26 mV
Full-bridge with opposite arms gives four times this: 5.04 mV
Note the output is small, so an instrumentation amplifier of gain 100–1000 follows
Mention that the full-bridge also cancels axial temperature effects
answer: Resistance change. ΔR = R·GF·ε = 120 × 2.1 × 600 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.1512 Ω, so the gauge reads 120.1512 Ω; ΔR/R = 1.26 × 10⁻³.

answer.text: Quarter bridge (one active arm). The other three arms are 120 Ω fixed resistors. Exactly, and by the small-strain formula:

answer: The approximate formula is high by only 0.06 % at this strain, so it is the one to use in an exam.
Half bridge. Two active arms, one in tension and one in compression, placed in adjacent arms: V0 = (Vs/2)·GF·ε = 2.52 mV, exactly linear.

answer.text: Full bridge (four active arms). Two gauges in tension in opposite arms, two in compression in the other opposite arms. Each change adds:
Comparison.

head: Arrangement
Active gauges
Output
Temperature compensation
rows: yes, and cancels lead and bending effects

answer: Amplification. Even the full-bridge 5.04 mV is small and rides on a 2 V common-mode level (half of Vs at each output corner). An instrumentation amplifier with high common-mode rejection and gain 500 gives 2.52 V for 600 µε, i.e. 4.2 mV/µε at the output.

Why the full bridge cancels temperature. A temperature change makes all four gauges change by the same ΔRT. In a bridge, equal changes in adjacent arms cancel, so only the strain, which has opposite signs in adjacent arms, appears.

Gauge heating. Each arm pair is 240 Ω across 4 V: I = 4/240 = 16.7 mA, P = I²R = 0.0167² × 120 = 33 mW per gauge, acceptable for a foil gauge on steel but too much on plastic or bone, where 1–2 V excitation would be chosen.
Check. 5.04/1.26 = 4.0, as expected for four active arms of equal strain magnitude.

bank.q: A Pt100 RTD has R<sub>0</sub> = 100 Ω at 0 °C. Find its resistance at 80 °C and the change in resistance per °C at that temperature, first with the linear law (α = 0.00385 /°C) and then with the Callendar–Van Dusen equation (A = 3.9083 × 10⁻³ /°C, B = −5.775 × 10⁻⁷ /°C², C = 0 above 0 °C). Suggest a bridge arrangement to read it.
outline: Slope dR/dT = R<sub>0</sub>(A + 2BT) = 0.3816 Ω/°C at 80 °C
The two laws differ by 0.10 Ω, about 0.25 °C
Three-wire bridge or a constant-current source with four-wire sensing
Lead resistance must be cancelled; keep the excitation current near 1 mA to limit self-heating
answer: Linear law. RT = R0(1 + αT) = 100(1 + 0.00385 × 80) = 100 × 1.308 = 130.80 Ω. Slope dR/dT = R0·α = 0.385 Ω/°C, the same at every temperature.

answer.text: Callendar–Van Dusen. Above 0 °C the C term is zero, so RT = R0(1 + AT + BT²):
Slope at 80 °C. Differentiate:

answer: Comparing the two. The linear law is 130.897 − 130.800 = 0.097 Ω low, which is 0.097/0.3816 = 0.25 °C. The linear α = 0.00385 is the average over 0–100 °C, so the two agree at 0 and 100 °C and differ slightly in between. Fractional sensitivity at 80 °C: 0.3816/130.9 = 0.29 %/°C.
Comparison with a thermistor. A 10 kΩ NTC (β = 3500 K) near 25 °C changes by about 390 Ω/°C, a thousand times more in ohms, but it is non-linear and could not reach the full RTD range.
The lead problem. If the RTD is 10 m away with 0.5 Ω per lead, a two-wire connection adds 1.0 Ω to the arm, which reads as 1.0/0.3816 = 2.6 °C too hot, and the leads drift with ambient temperature.

Three-wire bridge. One lead goes in series with the RTD arm, the second lead in series with the adjacent arm (the zero-set resistor of 100 Ω), and the third lead carries the detector connection, where no current flows. Lead resistance then appears in both adjacent arms and cancels at balance, and nearly cancels off balance.

answer.text: Bridge numbers. Equal 100 Ω arms, excitation 0.25 V, balanced at 0 °C:
answer.pre:
V<sub>0</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>[R<sub>T</sub>/(R<sub>T</sub> + 100) − 0.5] = 0.25 × (130.897/230.897 − 0.5) = 16.73 mV
RTD current = 0.25/230.9 = 1.08 mA
Sensitivity near 80 °C ≈ 0.18 mV/°C

answer: Better for precision: four-wire with constant current. Drive 1.000 mA through two leads and sense the voltage with the other two (no current, so no lead drop): 130.897 mV at 80 °C, 0.38 mV/°C. Self-heating is I²R = (10⁻³)² × 130.9 = 0.13 mW; with a dissipation constant of 5 mW/°C in stirred liquid the rise is only 0.03 °C.
Check. 100 × 1.308 = 130.80 Ω and 130.90 Ω differ by under 0.1 %; both are well within a Pt100 class A tolerance at 80 °C (±0.31 °C).

bank.q: A thermistor with B = 3900 K and R = 10 kΩ at 25 °C is used to measure 60 °C. Calculate its resistance, the resistance change per °C near 60 °C, and comment on the linearisation needed.
outline: R = R<sub>0</sub>·exp[β(1/T − 1/T<sub>0</sub>)] with T in kelvin (333.15 K and 298.15 K)
Exponent 3900 × that = −1.374, so R = 10 kΩ × 0.2530 = 2.53 kΩ
Sensitivity dR/dT = −(β/T²)·R = −88.9 Ω/°C, i.e. −3.51 %/°C
Nonlinearity handled by a parallel pad resistor, a lookup table or a log amplifier
Compare: an RTD at the same point changes by under 0.4 Ω/°C
answer: Given. β = 3900 K (the question’s B), R0 = 10 kΩ at T0 = 25 °C = 298.15 K; T = 60 °C = 333.15 K. Law: RT = R0·exp[β(1/T − 1/T0)].

answer.text: Resistance at 60 °C.
Sensitivity near 60 °C. Differentiating the law gives (1/R)(dR/dT) = −β/T²:

answer: Check by finite difference. R(59 °C) = 2621 Ω and R(61 °C) = 2443 Ω; (2443 − 2621)/2 = −89 Ω/°C, matching.

Nonlinearity. At 25 °C the fractional sensitivity is −3900/298.15² = −4.39 %/°C (−439 Ω/°C); at 60 °C it is −3.51 %/°C and only −89 Ω/°C. Across 40–80 °C the resistance falls from 5344 Ω to 1304 Ω, and the drop in the first ten degrees (1709 Ω) is three and a half times the drop in the last ten (495 Ω).

answer.text: Linearisation with a parallel pad. The parallel resistor that puts the inflection point of the combination at the mid-temperature Tm is Rp = Rm(β − 2Tm)/(β + 2Tm) = 2530 × (3900 − 666.3)/(3900 + 666.3) = 1792 Ω.

answer: The padded network changes by 142–151 Ω per 10 °C across the whole range, within about ±3 %, so a bridge or divider after it is nearly linear. The price is sensitivity: about −15 Ω/°C instead of −89 Ω/°C at 60 °C.

Other methods. A microcontroller lookup table or the Steinhart–Hart equation 1/T = a + b·ln R + c·(ln R)³ (best accuracy, no lost sensitivity); a logarithmic amplifier, since ln R is linear in 1/T; or a constant-current source with digital correction.

Comparison with an RTD. A Pt100 at 60 °C changes by about 0.38 Ω/°C, so the thermistor gives over 200 times more ohms per degree; that is why thermistors suit narrow ranges and small signals, such as body temperature.
Check. R must fall as T rises: 2530 Ω at 60 °C is below 10 kΩ at 25 °C, and the sign of dR/dT is negative.

bank.q: A constant-temperature hot-wire anemometer follows King’s law E² = A + B·u<sup>0.5</sup>, where E is the bridge output voltage and u the air speed. Two calibration points give E = 4.0 V at u = 0 and E = 6.0 V at u = 4 m/s. Predict E at 9 m/s and explain how the bridge holds the wire temperature constant.
outline: A = 16 V² from the zero-flow point
At u = 4 m/s, u<sup>0.5</sup> = 2, so 36 = 16 + 2B giving B = 10 V²/(m/s)<sup>0.5</sup>
Constant-temperature mode: the wire is one arm of a feedback bridge held at fixed resistance
Higher flow cools the wire, resistance falls, the amplifier raises the current to restore it
The output voltage is then a direct measure of cooling and hence of speed
Note the square-root law and the need for compensation of the air temperature
answer: Given. E² = A + B·u0.5; (u, E) = (0, 4.0 V) and (4 m/s, 6.0 V). Find A and B, then E at 9 m/s.

answer.text: Constants from calibration.
Prediction at 9 m/s.
The law is non-linear. Sensitivity dE/du = B/(4E·√u):

answer: Equal steps of speed give shrinking steps of voltage, so the instrument linearises digitally with u = [(E² − A)/B]². Check the inverse: E = 6.5 V gives √u = (42.25 − 16)/10 = 2.625, u = 6.89 m/s.

Physics of the wire. A fine tungsten or platinum wire, a few micrometres thick, is heated electrically to well above the air. Its heat balance is I²Rw = hA(Tw − Ta), and the convective coefficient h grows as a + b·u0.5; at constant Tw the electrical power, and so E², follows King’s law.

How the bridge holds the temperature constant. The wire is one arm of a Wheatstone bridge. The opposite arm is set so that the bridge balances when Rw is at its chosen hot value, for example 1.8 times its cold resistance (the overheat ratio). A high-gain amplifier senses the bridge imbalance and drives the bridge top.

The feedback loop. (1) Air speed rises. (2) The wire loses more heat and starts to cool. (3) Its resistance falls, unbalancing the bridge. (4) The amplifier raises the bridge voltage, pushing more current through the wire. (5) The wire reheats until Rw, and so Tw, returns to the set value. Because the wire temperature hardly moves, its thermal lag is bypassed and the response extends to tens of kilohertz. The bridge voltage E is the output.

Air temperature compensation. E² is proportional to Tw − Ta. With a 200 °C overheat, air 2 °C warmer than at calibration scales E² by 198/200 = 0.99: at 9 m/s E becomes 6.748 V, which the old calibration reads as 8.73 m/s, a 3 % error. A second, unheated wire in the bridge, or a separate temperature reading, corrects it.
Biomedical use. The same principle measures breathing flow in ventilators and spirometers, where a heated wire or film in the airway gives a fast flow signal.
Check. 6.78 V lies between 6.0 V at 4 m/s and the 7.48 V that the law gives at 16 m/s, and the 2.25-fold rise in speed from 4 to 9 m/s gives only 13 % more voltage.

bank.q: Analyse the sources of error in a bonded strain-gauge installation and evaluate the correction used for each: lead-wire resistance, temperature change of the gauge and the test piece, creep, and moisture.
outline: Lead resistance adds to the arm and reduces sensitivity: use three-wire or full-bridge connection
Apparent strain from differential expansion: use a dummy gauge or a self-temperature-compensated gauge
Resistivity and modulus both change with temperature: bridge has to cancel both
Creep and hysteresis from the adhesive and the carrier: choose correct adhesive and cure cycle
Moisture changes insulation resistance: use encapsulated gauges
Nonlinearity of semiconductor gauges and their strong temperature coefficient
answer: Approach. For each source, state how it appears in the reading, estimate its size for a 120 Ω foil gauge with GF = 2.0, and evaluate the usual correction.

answer.text: 1. Lead-wire resistance. With a two-wire quarter bridge and 10 m of cable at 0.1 Ω/m, each lead is 1 Ω and the arm carries 2 Ω extra.
answer.pre:
Sensitivity loss = R/(R + R<sub>L</sub>) = 120/122 = 0.984  →  1.6 % low
Leads warming by 10 °C: ΔR = 0.0039 × 2 × 10 = 0.078 Ω
Apparent strain = ΔR/(R·GF) = 0.078/(120 × 2) = 325 µε

answer: Correction: the three-wire connection puts one lead in the gauge arm and one in the adjacent arm, so equal lead changes cancel; the third lead carries no current. A half or full bridge with all gauges at the site, and remote sensing of the excitation, removes the remaining sensitivity loss. Evaluation: three-wire is cheap and effective; the residual is only the mismatch between leads.

2. Temperature: apparent strain. A temperature change alters the gauge resistance (its temperature coefficient of resistance) and, if the gauge alloy and the test piece expand differently, strains the gauge with no load. Apparent strain ≈ [αR/GF + (αs − αg)]·ΔT, with αs and αg the expansion coefficients of specimen and gauge. A gauge matched to steel (11 × 10⁻⁶/°C) on aluminium (23 × 10⁻⁶/°C) sees about 12 µε per °C; 10 °C gives 120 µε of false strain.

Corrections: (a) a self-temperature-compensated gauge whose alloy is heat-treated to match the specimen’s expansion; (b) a dummy gauge on an unloaded piece of the same material at the same temperature, in the adjacent bridge arm, so its change cancels; (c) a half or full bridge with active gauges at opposite strain, which cancels temperature and doubles or quadruples the signal. Evaluation: (c) is best where the geometry allows; (a) is the standard for single gauges; (b) needs a truly identical environment.

3. Temperature: gauge factor and modulus. Even with the zero compensated, GF changes slightly with temperature, and in a load cell the elastic modulus of the element falls as it warms, so the same load gives more strain. Correction: span-compensation resistors (often nickel) in series with the bridge supply, trimmed during temperature cycling. Evaluation: only worthwhile in transducers; in stress analysis the error is small for constantan.

4. Creep and hysteresis. Under a steady load the adhesive and the carrier relax, so the reading drifts slowly downward; on unloading it does not return exactly. Causes: soft or under-cured adhesive, thick glue lines, high temperature. Corrections: a proper strain-gauge adhesive (cyanoacrylate for short tests, epoxy with the specified cure and post-cure for transducers), thin even glue lines, and gauges whose grid end-loops are designed to balance the creep of the element. Evaluation: essential for long-term weighing; a load cell is specified for creep over 30 minutes at full load.

answer.text: 5. Moisture. Water absorbed by the adhesive and carrier lowers the insulation resistance between grid and specimen, which appears as a shunt across the gauge:
answer.pre:
Shunt at 10 MΩ: ΔR ≈ R²/R<sub>sh</sub> = 120²/10⁷ = 1.44 mΩ  →  6 µε
Shunt at 1 MΩ:  ΔR ≈ 120²/10⁶ = 14.4 mΩ  →  60 µε, and drifting

answer: Moisture also swells the adhesive and corrodes the grid. Corrections: dry the surface before bonding, check insulation resistance with a megohmmeter after curing, and seal the installation with a protective coating (silicone rubber, polyurethane or wax, with a metal-foil cover outdoors). Evaluation: cheap to prevent, impossible to correct after it starts.

6. Semiconductor gauges. Their GF of 100 or more makes the signal large, but GF varies with strain (non-linear) and both GF and resistance change strongly with temperature. Corrections: matched pairs of p-type and n-type elements in a bridge, constant-current excitation, and digital correction.

answer.text: Summary.

answer: Check. The two largest errors here (325 µε and 120 µε) are both temperature effects, and both are removed by a full bridge with three-wire or local connection, which is why transducers use one.

bank.q: An invasive blood-pressure transducer must read arterial pressure from −50 to 300 mmHg through a saline-filled catheter. Design the measurement chain: elastic element, gauge placement, bridge configuration, excitation, amplification and calibration. Justify each choice.
outline: Thin circular diaphragm as the elastic element, fluid-coupled to the catheter through a dome
Four gauges, two near the centre in tension and two near the edge in compression, forming a full bridge
Full bridge gives four times the quarter-bridge output and cancels temperature effects
Excitation of about 5 V, at a rated sensitivity of 5 µV/V/mmHg, giving 25 µV/mmHg
Isolated instrumentation amplifier with high common-mode rejection, then a low-pass filter
Zero to atmosphere at heart level, then check span against a reference manometer
Overpressure protection against flush pressures and patient isolation
answer: Requirement. Range −50 to 300 mmHg, resolution about 1 mmHg, bandwidth to about 20 Hz (the first ten harmonics of a heart rate of 120 per minute), safe connection to a patient, and a single-use sterile sensor.

Elastic element. A thin circular diaphragm, clamped at its edge, inside a plastic dome filled with saline that connects to the arterial catheter. Pressure bends the diaphragm a few micrometres. Justification: a diaphragm converts pressure to surface strain directly, is small (a few millimetres across, so little fluid volume moves and the catheter system stays stiff), and is cheap to make as a silicon chip.

Gauge placement. On a clamped diaphragm the surface near the centre is stretched (positive strain) and near the edge it is compressed, with the edge strain about twice the centre value in magnitude. Two gauges go near the centre and two near the edge. In a disposable transducer they are piezoresistors diffused into the silicon diaphragm, GF around 100, rather than foil, so the strain needed is tiny.

Bridge configuration. Full Wheatstone bridge: the two centre gauges in opposite arms, the two edge gauges in the other opposite arms. Justification: every gauge adds to the output (four times a quarter bridge); a temperature change, which shifts all four equally, cancels; and the output is zero at zero pressure without a large standing offset.

answer.text: Excitation and signal. The standard rating is 5 µV per volt of excitation per mmHg. At 5 V:
answer.pre:
Sensitivity = 5 µV/V/mmHg × 5 V = 25 µV/mmHg
120 mmHg → 3.0 mV;  300 mmHg → 7.5 mV;  −50 mmHg → −1.25 mV

answer: Justification for 5 V: it gives a usable millivolt signal while bridge heating stays low; with arms of about 1 kΩ each gauge has 2.5 V across it and dissipates 2.5²/1000 = 6.25 mW. Ratiometric conversion, with the ADC reference taken from the excitation, removes drift of the supply.

answer.text: Amplification. An isolated instrumentation amplifier with high common-mode rejection (the output rides on 2.5 V), gain 300, and a 0.5 V offset for the negative range, then a low-pass filter at about 40 Hz:
answer.pre:
Output = 300 × 25 µV/mmHg = 7.5 mV/mmHg
−50 mmHg → 0.5 − 0.375 = 0.125 V;  300 mmHg → 0.5 + 2.25 = 2.75 V
12-bit ADC on 3.3 V: 0.806 mV per step = 0.11 mmHg

answer: Patient safety. The front end is electrically isolated from mains earth (an isolation barrier with leakage current in the microampere range), because the saline column is a conducting path to the heart. The transducer must also survive flush and syringe pressures far above 300 mmHg, so the diaphragm is designed with an overpressure margin and a mechanical stop.

Calibration. (1) Level the transducer at the phlebostatic axis (heart level); every 10 cm of height error adds 10 cmH2O = 7.4 mmHg. (2) Open the stopcock to air and zero. (3) Check the span against a reference manometer at, say, 100 and 200 mmHg: 100 mmHg must read 2.5 mV at the bridge (0.75 V above offset at the amplifier). (4) Do a fast-flush test to check the catheter’s natural frequency and damping, since a stiff, well-damped line is needed for a true waveform.

answer.text: Design summary.

head: Stage
Choice
Reason
rows: small volume, direct pressure to strain
opposite strains add in a bridge
zero at heart level, two-point span, flush test

answer: Check. A typical arterial pressure of 120/80 mmHg gives 3.0/2.0 mV at the bridge and 1.40/1.10 V at the amplifier output, inside the 0–3.3 V ADC range.

bank.q: Compare a thermocouple, an RTD and a thermistor for measuring a patient's body temperature in the range 35–42 °C in a hospital setting. Evaluate sensitivity, linearity, safety, size and cost, and state your recommendation.
outline: Range is narrow, so the sensor must resolve 0.1 °C or better
Thermistor: fast, small, high sensitivity, cheap; needs linearisation and has drift
RTD: stable and repeatable, good for calibration reference, but larger and slower
Thermocouple: robust and tiny but needs a cold junction and its sensitivity is low near body temperature
Excitation and self-heating must be limited to keep the probe from warming the tissue
Recommendation: thermistor in a disposable probe for routine use, RTD for a reference thermometer
answer: Requirement. Range 35–42 °C, resolution 0.1 °C or better, accuracy about ±0.1 °C, a probe small enough for the mouth, rectum, oesophagus or skin, electrically safe, and cheap enough to be single-use or covered.

Thermistor (NTC, 10 kΩ at 25 °C, β = 3500 K). R(35 °C) = 6832 Ω, R(37 °C) = 6350 Ω, R(42 °C) = 5309 Ω. Sensitivity at 37 °C: −β/T² = −3500/310.15² = −3.64 %/°C, so −231 Ω/°C and −23 Ω per 0.1 °C. With 100 µA excitation that is 2.3 mV per 0.1 °C, easy to resolve.

Thermistor: other points. Non-linear, but over 7 °C the curve is gentle and a lookup table or Steinhart–Hart fit handles it. Interchangeable thermistors are matched to ±0.1–0.2 °C. Bead or chip sizes under 1 mm give time constants of a second or two. Very cheap, so disposable probes are practical. Drift is small after ageing but must be checked.

RTD (Pt100). R(37 °C) = 100(1 + 0.00385 × 37) = 114.2 Ω; sensitivity 0.385 Ω/°C, 0.0385 Ω per 0.1 °C. At 1 mA that is only 38.5 µV per 0.1 °C. Excellent linearity, stability and repeatability; the element and sheath are larger and slower; cost is higher. The standard for a reference or calibration thermometer.

Thermocouple (type T, copper–constantan). About 41 µV/°C near 37 °C, so 0.1 °C is 4.1 µV, close to amplifier offset and noise. It needs cold-junction compensation accurate to better than 0.1 °C, since a cold-junction error passes straight to the reading. Very small and robust; used in needle probes and catheters for tissue or hyperthermia studies, not routine bedside temperature.

answer.text: Self-heating and safety. Excitation must not warm the probe or tissue:
answer.pre:
Thermistor at 100 µA: P = (10⁻⁴)² × 6350 = 63.5 µW; in tissue at δ ≈ 2 mW/°C → 0.03 °C
Pt100 at 1 mA: P = (10⁻³)² × 114.2 = 0.11 mW → about 0.06 °C
Thermocouple: no excitation, no self-heating

answer: Electrical safety: the probe touches the patient, so the measuring circuit must be isolated and the leakage current kept in the microampere range; a low-voltage, low-current sensor helps. Probes in contact with mucous membranes are covered by a disposable sheath or are themselves disposable.

answer.text: Comparison.

answer: Recommendation. A thermistor in a disposable or sheathed probe for routine patient monitoring, because it gives the largest signal for 0.1 °C, is small and fast, and is cheap. A platinum RTD for the reference thermometer used to check the thermistor probes. A thermocouple only where a needle-sized probe or a very fast response inside tissue is needed.
Check. The thermistor signal for 0.1 °C (2.3 mV) is about 60 times that of the Pt100 (38.5 µV) and over 500 times that of the thermocouple (4.1 µV).

bank.q: Evaluate four methods of cold-junction compensation for a thermocouple measuring a furnace at about 900 °C: ice bath, isothermal block with a semiconductor sensor, bridge circuit with a temperature-sensitive resistor, and software compensation with a stored table.
outline: Ice bath: most accurate reference but impractical for plant use
Isothermal block with a thermistor or IC sensor: standard practice, good to about 0.5 °C
Compensating bridge in the instrument: simple but drifts and is hard to make accurate
Software with an ITS-90 table and a measured cold-junction value: flexible and now the norm
Also consider extension leads and their own thermoelectric voltages, and the law of intermediate metals
Conclusion: cold-junction error of 1 °C is a real error of about 1 °C at the hot junction because the emf is linear in the difference
answer: Why compensation is needed. A thermocouple measures E(Th, Tc), not Th. With type K at 900 °C and the cold junction at 25 °C, table values give E(900, 0) = 37.326 mV and E(25, 0) = 1.000 mV, so the meter sees 36.326 mV. Read directly from the table this is 875 °C, 25 °C low. Every method below supplies the missing 1.000 mV (law of intermediate temperatures).

1. Ice bath. The reference junctions sit in a flask of crushed ice and pure water at 0 °C, so the reading is E(Th, 0) directly and the table applies with no correction. Merits: the most accurate reference, within about 0.1 °C if the ice is made properly and kept stirred; no electronics. Demerits: the ice melts, needs attention and cannot be used on a plant or in a portable instrument. Use: calibration laboratories.

2. Isothermal block with a semiconductor sensor. The thermocouple wires end on terminals mounted on a copper or aluminium block that keeps both terminals at one temperature (law of intermediate metals). A thermistor, RTD or IC temperature sensor on the block measures Tc, and the circuit adds E(Tc, 0). Merits: standard practice in transmitters and data loggers, typically good to about 0.5 °C. Demerits: the block must really be isothermal; heat from nearby electronics or a draught causes gradients.

3. Compensating bridge. A Wheatstone bridge in series with the thermocouple has one arm that is a temperature-sensitive resistor (copper or nickel) at the cold junction. As Tc rises the bridge output rises by about S·ΔTc, cancelling the loss in thermocouple emf. Merits: simple and analogue, needs no processor. Demerits: the resistor is near linear while the thermocouple emf is not, so it is exact only near its design temperature; it must be matched to one thermocouple type; the bridge supply and resistors drift. Errors of about 1 °C or more are common away from the design ambient.

4. Software compensation. The processor measures Tc on the block, converts it to E(Tc, 0) with the ITS-90 reference polynomial for the type in use, adds the measured emf, and inverts the polynomial to get Th. Merits: handles any thermocouple type by changing the table, is exact for the curve, and allows linearisation and diagnostics; it is now the norm. Demerits: still depends on the accuracy of the block sensor.

answer.text: Working for software compensation.
answer.pre:
Measured emf = 36.326 mV; block sensor reads T<sub>c</sub> = 25.0 °C
E(25, 0) from the polynomial = 1.000 mV
E(T<sub>h</sub>, 0) = 36.326 + 1.000 = 37.326 mV  →  inverse polynomial  →  T<sub>h</sub> = 900.0 °C

answer: Cold-junction error passes straight through. If the block sensor reads 26 °C instead of 25 °C, the added emf is 1.041 mV, and the result is 901.0 °C. A 1 °C cold-junction error gives about a 1 °C error at 900 °C (1.01 °C, since the type K slope is 40.5 µV/°C at 25 °C and 40.0 µV/°C at 900 °C). The cold-junction sensor’s accuracy is a floor under the whole measurement.

Extension leads. The junction head on a furnace may be at 60 °C while the instrument is at 25 °C. If plain copper wire ran from the head, the cold junction would be at 60 °C but compensated as 25 °C: the reading would be E(900) − E(60) + E(25) = 37.326 − 2.436 + 1.000 = 35.890 mV, about 864 °C, 36 °C low. Type K extension cable (same alloys) carries the cold junction to the instrument block. Reversing its polarity at one end gives a large error, about twice the emf between head and instrument.

answer.text: Evaluation.

answer: Conclusion. For a 900 °C furnace the choice is an isothermal block with a good sensor and software compensation, fed by correct type K extension cable. At 900 °C the type K tolerance itself (±0.75 % of reading, about ±6.8 °C for standard grade) is larger than the 0.5 °C compensation error, so the cold junction is no longer the weakest link.

glossary.def: Change in length divided by original length of a body, a dimensionless number usually quoted in microstrain (10⁻⁶).
Ratio of sideways contraction to lengthwise extension of a stretched material, about 0.3 for steel and aluminium.
Change of a material's resistivity caused by mechanical stress, the effect that gives semiconductor gauges their large gauge factor.
Active length of the resistance grid along the measuring axis; strain is averaged over this length.
The DC or AC supply voltage or current fed to a Wheatstone bridge, which sets the size of the output signal.
Bridge arrangements with one, two or four active gauge arms, giving output in the ratio 1 : 2 : 4.
An unstrained gauge mounted on the same material and placed in the adjacent bridge arm to cancel temperature effects.
Rise in a sensor's own temperature caused by the measuring current, an error source in RTDs and thermistors.
Fractional change of resistance per degree Celsius, 0.00385 /°C for platinum and negative and large for an NTC thermistor.
RTD wiring in which the lead resistances cancel in the bridge, leaving only the sensor resistance.
Slow change of sensor output under a steady load, caused by the adhesive or the elastic element settling.
Difference between the readings taken while loading and while unloading, for the same applied quantity.
Change in output divided by the change in input that caused it, with units such as V/mm or Ω/°C.
Difference between the upper and lower limits of the measurable range of a sensor.
The sliding contact of a potentiometer that taps a fraction of the track and carries the output voltage.
Water vapour actually present in air as a percentage of the maximum the air can hold at that temperature.
Emf produced per degree of junction temperature difference, quoted in µV/°C and specific to each metal pair.
The thermocouple junction held at a known temperature, whose value must be added to the measured emf.
Several thermocouples in series to multiply the emf, used in radiation sensors and gas detectors.
Any circuit or software step that converts a curved sensor characteristic into a straight line over the working range.
Maximum deviation of the sensor output from the best straight line, expressed as a percentage of full-scale output.
Negative temperature coefficient thermistor, whose resistance falls as temperature rises.
Instrument for measuring fluid flow speed; the hot-wire form uses the cooling of a heated resistor.
Light-dependent resistor, another name for a photoresistor used in light-operated switches and exposure meters.
Fine wires stretched between a frame and a moving armature, straining directly without being glued to a surface.
A joint-angle sensor, often a rotary potentiometer strapped across the joint.
